problems.title: Three constraints at one wing loading
problems.setup: A jet trainer is sized at W_TO/S = 4000 Pa. Takeoff: sea level (α = β = 1), C_Lmax = 2.0, ground roll s_G = 1000 m, liftoff speed 1.2V_stall, drag and rolling friction neglected. Cruise: q = 12,000 Pa, C_D0 = 0.02, K = 0.05, β = 0.95, α = 0.35. Sustained turn: same q, α, β, C_D0, K at n = 3. Use ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s².

parts.ask: Find T_SL/W_TO for the takeoff constraint (3 decimals).
sol: Simplified takeoff: T_SL/W_TO = (β²/α)k_TO²(W_TO/S)/(ρ g C_Lmax s_G)

parts.ask: Find T_SL/W_TO for the cruise constraint (3 decimals).
Find T_SL/W_TO for the n = 3 sustained turn (3 decimals).
sol: Turn: the induced term carries n²: Kn²β(W_TO/S)/q = 0.05·9·3800/12,000

parts.ask: Which constraint sets the engine size at W_TO/S = 4000 Pa?
w: The takeoff roll, at T_SL/W_TO ≈ 0.24
The cruise, at T_SL/W_TO ≈ 0.21
All three tie at T_SL/W_TO ≈ 0.24
sol: Required T_SL/W_TO is the largest of the constraint values: max(0.240, 0.214, 0.558)
The turn needs 0.558, so the turn is the active constraint at this wing loading

problems.x: At a chosen wing loading the design thrust loading is the highest of all constraint curves, and the n² induced term makes turn requirements dominate for maneuvering aircraft.

problems.title: Turn bucket versus landing stall limit
problems.setup: A fighter must sustain an n = 2 turn at q = 15,000 Pa with β = 0.9, α = 0.6, C_D0 = 0.018, K = 0.06. It must also land with V_stall ≤ 50 m/s at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³), C_Lmax = 2.2, at a landing weight fraction β_L = 0.85. The turn constraint is T_SL/W_TO = (β/α)[qC_D0/(βW_TO/S) + Kn²β(W_TO/S)/q].

parts.ask: Find the largest W_TO/S allowed by the landing stall constraint (Pa).
sol: W_TO/S = 3368.75/0.85 = 3963 Pa (a vertical line on the diagram)

parts.ask: Find the W_TO/S at the bottom of the turn bucket (Pa).
Find the minimum T_SL/W_TO at the bucket (3 decimals).
sol: At the bucket the parasite and induced terms are equal, each n√(KC_D0)

parts.ask: The stall limit sits left of the bucket, so the design point is at the stall-limited W_TO/S. Find T_SL/W_TO there (3 decimals).

problems.x: The design point is the lowest feasible T/W inside all constraints, so a stall line left of the turn bucket pins W/S and costs a little extra thrust.

problems.title: Business jet stall, L/D and range
problems.setup: A business jet has W = 100 kN, S = 30 m², parabolic polar C_D = 0.022 + 0.045C_L², clean C_Lmax = 1.6. It cruises at V = 230 m/s with TSFC c = 0.6 1/h, average L/D = 15, and W_initial/W_final = 1.25. Use ρ_SL = 1.225 kg/m³.

parts.ask: Find the sea-level stall speed (m/s).
Find (L/D)_max (2 decimals).
Find the Breguet range (km, nearest 10).
For maximum jet range at a fixed altitude, the aircraft should fly at which condition?
w: Max C_L/C_D, where C_D0 = KC_L²
Max C_L^1.5/C_D, where 3C_D0 = KC_L²
Min drag speed times √3, where C_L = 3C_D0

problems.x: Jet range at fixed altitude is driven by V·L/D, so the best range speed is 1.32 times the minimum drag speed at √C_L/C_D maximum.

problems.title: Piston aircraft power required and climb
problems.setup: A piston propeller aircraft weighs W = 12,000 N with S = 16 m², C_D = 0.03 + 0.06C_L², flying at altitude where ρ = 1.0 kg/m³. The engine delivers 100 kW of shaft power at all speeds of interest and propeller efficiency is η_p = 0.8.

parts.ask: Find the speed for minimum power required (m/s).
sol: Minimum P_R at max C_L^1.5/C_D, where 3C_D0 = KC_L²

parts.ask: Find the minimum power required (kW).
Find the maximum rate of climb (m/s, 2 decimals).
sol: With constant P_A, excess power peaks where P_R is least

parts.ask: Explain why a turbojet's best climb speed is higher than this piston aircraft's.
parts.a: Jet thrust is roughly constant with speed, so power available rises linearly with V, and the peak of P_A − P_R moves to a speed above the minimum drag speed. The piston aircraft has nearly constant power available, so its best climb sits at the minimum power required speed.
sol: Prop: P_A ≈ constant, so max excess power is at min P_R
Jet: P_A = TV grows with V, so best climb speed rises above V_md

problems.x: Maximum rate of climb is the largest specific excess power (P_A − P_R)/W, which for constant power available falls at the minimum power speed.

problems.title: Corner speed and gust check for a transport
problems.setup: A transport has W/S = 3500 Pa, C_Lmax = 1.4 and positive limit load factor n = 3.8 (sea level, ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³). At cruise speed V_C = 150 m/s EAS it must meet a derived gust U_de = 15.24 m/s with wing lift slope a = 5.5 /rad and gust alleviation factor K_g = 0.75.

parts.ask: Find the corner (maneuvering) speed V_A (m/s).
sol: At V_A the stall curve n = ρV²C_Lmax/(2W/S) meets n_limit

parts.ask: Find the 1g stall speed (m/s).
Find the total gust load factor n = 1 + Δn at V_C (2 decimals).
Which case sets the positive design load for this transport?
parts.a: Maneuver, since 3.8 exceeds the gust value
w: Gust, since gusts always govern transports
Gust, since Δn exceeds the limit load
Stall, since V_C lies below V_A
sol: The envelope takes the larger value, so the maneuver limit sets the design load here

problems.x: The V-n envelope is the outer boundary of maneuver and gust lines, and high wing loading keeps the gust increment below the maneuver limit.

problems.title: Light aircraft where gusts govern
problems.setup: A very light aircraft has W/S = 600 Pa, mean chord c̄ = 1.5 m, wing lift slope a = 5.0 /rad and limit maneuver load factor 3.8. At V_C = 60 m/s EAS it meets U_de = 15.24 m/s at sea level (ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²). Use μ_g = 2(W/S)/(ρc̄ag) and K_g = 0.88μ_g/(5.3 + μ_g).

parts.ask: Find the mass ratio μ_g (2 decimals).
Find the gust alleviation factor K_g (3 decimals).
Find the gust load factor n = 1 + Δn (2 decimals).
What follows for the structural design load?
w: Maneuver sets it, at 3.8
Gust sets it, at about 2.94
Neither, since stall caps n at 1
sol: Gust n = 3.94 exceeds the maneuver limit 3.8
Low W/S means a large Δn per unit gust, so gusts govern light aircraft and sailplanes

problems.x: Gust load increment scales as V/(W/S), so lightly loaded aircraft at cruise speed see gust loads that exceed the maneuver limit.

problems.title: Ideal turbofan stations and fan stream efficiency
problems.setup: An ideal separate-flow turbofan flies at M₀ = 0.8 with T₀ = 220 K. Overall core pressure ratio π_c = 25 (includes the fan), fan pressure ratio π_f = 1.6, bypass ratio 5, T_t4 = 1500 K. Use γ = 1.4, c_p = 1004.5 J/(kg·K), R = 287 J/(kg·K), neglect fuel mass, and expand both nozzles fully to p₀.

parts.ask: Find the compressor exit total temperature T_t3 (K).
The turbine drives the core compressor and the fan. Find the turbine exit total temperature T_t5 (K).
Find the propulsive efficiency of the bypass stream (3 decimals).
sol: Ideal full expansion gives T₁₉ = T₀, so V₁₉ = √(2c_p(T_t13 − T₀)) = 358.1 m/s

parts.ask: At fixed T_t4 and π_c, raising bypass ratio with a lower fan pressure ratio mainly:
w: Raises specific thrust and η_th
Lowers η_p and raises TSFC
Raises T_t4 at the same fuel flow
sol: A larger, slower jet gives exhaust velocity closer to V₀, so η_p = 2/(1 + V_e/V₀) rises
η_th is set by the cycle, so overall efficiency rises and TSFC falls

problems.x: In an ideal turbofan the turbine supplies both core and fan work, and a slow, high-mass bypass jet gives high propulsive efficiency.

problems.title: Ideal turbojet thermal, propulsive and overall efficiency
problems.setup: An ideal turbojet flies at M₀ = 2.0, T₀ = 216.7 K with compressor pressure ratio π_c = 10 and γ = 1.4. The nozzle exit velocity is 1.6 times flight speed (V₉/V₀ = 1.6) and fuel mass is neglected.

parts.ask: Find the ideal Brayton thermal efficiency η_th (3 decimals).
sol: Total cycle pressure ratio π_rπ_c gives η_th = 1 − 1/(τ_rτ_c)

parts.ask: Find the propulsive efficiency η_p (3 decimals).
Find the overall efficiency η_o (3 decimals).
At fixed T_t4, sweeping π_c upward from 1 toward very high values:
parts.a: Raises η_th; specific thrust peaks then falls
w: Lowers η_th; specific thrust rises without limit
Leaves η_th fixed; specific thrust rises steadily
Raises η_th and specific thrust together without limit
sol: With T_t4 capped, heat added per kg shrinks as T_t3 rises, so specific thrust peaks at τ_c = √(τ_λ)/τ_r and then falls

problems.x: Overall efficiency is the product of thermal efficiency, set by cycle pressure ratio including ram, and propulsive efficiency, set by V_e/V₀.

problems.title: Elliptic wing induced drag and root moment
problems.setup: A high aspect ratio UAV has an elliptically loaded wing, span b = 12 m, area S = 12 m², weight W = 8000 N, flying level at V = 40 m/s where ρ = 1.1 kg/m³. Treat lift = weight, carried entirely by the wing.

parts.ask: Find the lift coefficient (3 decimals).
Find the induced drag (N).
sol: Check: D_i = L²/(πqb²) gives the same value

parts.ask: Find the root bending moment of one semispan (N·m).
sol: Each semispan carries L/2, its elliptic load centroid sits at 4(b/2)/(3π) = 2b/(3π)

parts.ask: Span grows 20% at the same lift and dynamic pressure, loading still elliptic. What happens?
parts.a: D_i falls to 0.69×, root moment rises 1.2×
w: D_i falls to 0.83×, root moment rises 1.44×
D_i falls to 0.69×, root moment holds fixed
D_i falls to 0.83×, root moment rises 1.2×
sol: M_root = Lb/(3π) ∝ b, so 1.2×: span buys induced drag with structural weight

problems.x: Induced drag depends on span loading L/b, while root bending grows with span, which is the core aero-structural span trade.

problems.title: Finite wing lift slope and induced drag
problems.setup: A wing uses an airfoil with a₀ = 6.0 /rad and zero lift angle α_L0 = −2°. The wing has AR = 9 and span efficiency e = 0.95 (use e in both the lift slope and induced drag formulas). It flies at geometric angle of attack α = 4°.

parts.ask: Find the wing lift slope a (/rad, 3 decimals).
Find the wing lift coefficient (3 decimals).
Find the induced drag coefficient (5 decimals).
Explain physically why the finite wing lift slope is lower than a₀.
parts.a: Trailing vortices induce a downwash at the wing that tilts the local flow, so each section sees an effective angle α − α_i that is smaller than the geometric angle. The induced angle grows with C_L and shrinks with aspect ratio, so lower AR gives a lower lift slope.
sol: Downwash from the trailing vortex system lowers effective α
α_i = C_L/(πeAR), so the reduction is largest at low AR

problems.x: Downwash from the trailing vortex sheet lowers the effective angle of attack, reducing lift slope and tilting lift back to create induced drag.

problems.title: Hover power on Earth and Mars
problems.setup: A 1.8 kg rotorcraft is modeled as a single equivalent rotor disk of radius R = 0.6 m. Earth: g = 9.81 m/s², ρ = 1.225 kg/m³. Mars: g = 3.71 m/s², ρ = 0.017 kg/m³. Use ideal momentum theory P = T^(3/2)/√(2ρA) with thrust equal to weight.

parts.ask: Find the ideal hover power on Earth (W).
Find the ideal hover power on Mars (W).
Find the induced velocity at the Mars disk (m/s).
With figure of merit 0.6, find the actual Mars hover power (W).

problems.x: Ideal hover power scales as T^1.5/√ρ, so Mars's thin air outweighs its lower gravity and demands about twice the Earth hover power for the same vehicle.

problems.title: Helicopter forward flight limits
problems.setup: A helicopter main rotor has radius R = 6 m and tip speed ΩR = 200 m/s. It flies forward at V = 70 m/s where the speed of sound is 340 m/s. Use the advance ratio μ = V/(ΩR) (small shaft tilt).

parts.ask: Find the advance ratio μ (3 decimals).
Find the advancing tip Mach number (3 decimals).
sol: Advancing tip (ψ = 90°) speed = ΩR + V = 270 m/s

parts.ask: Find the diameter of the reverse flow circle on the retreating side (m).
sol: Reverse flow where Ωr + V sinψ < 0; at ψ = 270° it spans 0 < r < μR
The region is a circle of diameter μR centered at r = μR/2 on the retreating side

parts.ask: Which pair of effects bounds the top speed of this helicopter?
parts.a: Advancing tip compressibility and retreating blade stall
w: Retreating tip compressibility and advancing blade stall
Ground effect loss and vortex ring state
Autorotation and dissymmetry of hover inflow
sol: Advancing tip Mach (ΩR + V)/a rises toward drag divergence
Retreating side has low dynamic pressure, so blades there need high α to balance roll and they stall

problems.x: Forward speed is bounded on the advancing side by tip Mach number and on the retreating side by blade stall and the growing reverse flow region.

problems.title: Typical section divergence
problems.setup: A typical section has torsional stiffness k_θ = 5×10⁴ N·m/rad at the elastic axis, area S = 2 m², lift slope C_Lα = 2π /rad, and its aerodynamic center lies e = 0.1 m ahead of the elastic axis. Rigid incidence is α₀ = 2°. Use ρ = 1.225 kg/m³.

parts.ask: Find the divergence dynamic pressure q_D (Pa).
sol: Moment balance: k_θθ = qSeC_Lα(α₀ + θ); twist grows without bound at q_D = k_θ/(SeC_Lα)

parts.ask: Find the sea-level divergence speed (m/s).
At q = q_D/2, find the elastic twist θ (deg).
Which change raises q_D?
parts.a: Moving the elastic axis forward toward the AC
w: Moving the elastic axis aft of its current place
Raising the lift slope C_Lα
Raising the wing area S at fixed k_θ
sol: q_D = k_θ/(SeC_Lα) rises as e falls
With the elastic axis at the AC (e = 0), lift acts through the elastic axis and q_D becomes infinite

problems.x: Divergence occurs where the aerodynamic twisting stiffness qSeC_Lα equals the structural stiffness k_θ, so q_D grows with k_θ and with a smaller AC offset e.

problems.title: Transport takeoff weight iteration
problems.setup: A jet transport carries crew plus payload of 22,000 lb. Mission: warmup and takeoff 0.97, climb 0.985, cruise R = 5000 km at V = 864 km/h, TSFC c = 0.5 1/h, L/D = 16, landing 0.995, with 6% reserve and trapped fuel. Empty weight fraction W_e/W_0 = 1.02W_0^(−0.06) (W_0 in lb).

parts.ask: Find the cruise weight fraction W₃/W₂ (4 decimals).
Find W_f/W_0 (4 decimals).
Iterate to the converged W_0 (lb, nearest 100).
sol: Guess W_0, compute W_e/W_0 = 1.02W_0^(−0.06), update W_0, repeat

parts.ask: Why does each added pound of payload raise W_0 by several pounds?
parts.a: Fuel and structure fractions scale with W_0
w: Payload adds parasite drag that Breguet ignores
Empty weight fraction rises as W_0 grows
Reserve fuel is a fixed absolute weight
sol: W_0 = W_p/(1 − W_f/W_0 − W_e/W_0): every pound of W_0 drags along fuel and structure
Since W_e/W_0 falls slowly as W_0 grows, the marginal growth is ∂W_0/∂W_p ≈ 3.4 lb per lb

problems.x: Takeoff weight is payload divided by the useful-load fraction left after fuel and empty weight, which makes W_0 highly sensitive to payload and mission range.

problems.title: Steady climbing coordinated turn
problems.setup: An aircraft flies a steady, coordinated climbing turn at V = 150 m/s, flight path angle γ = 10°, bank angle φ = 45°, g = 9.81 m/s². Use point-mass wind-axis equations with thrust along the velocity: L cos φ = W cos γ and mV cos γ ψ̇ = L sin φ.

parts.ask: Find the load factor n = L/W (3 decimals).
sol: Normal equation with γ̇ = 0: L cos φ = W cos γ

parts.ask: Find the turn rate ψ̇ (deg/s, 2 decimals).
sol: ψ̇ = L sin φ/(mV cos γ) = ng sin φ/(V cos γ); substitute n = cos γ/cos φ

parts.ask: Find the radius of the horizontal ground track (m).
sol: Horizontal speed V cos γ = 147.7 m/s

parts.ask: Compared with a level turn at the same V and φ, this climbing turn has:
w: Larger n, larger turn rate
Same n, smaller turn rate
Smaller n, smaller turn rate
sol: Level: n = 1/cos φ = 1.414; climbing: n = cos γ/cos φ = 1.393
ψ̇ = g tan φ/V in both cases, so turn rate depends only on V and φ

problems.x: In a steady coordinated turn, n cos φ = cos γ sets the load factor and the turn rate is g tan φ/V for any climb angle.

problems.title: Energy height and specific excess power
problems.setup: A fighter at h = 6000 m flies at V = 250 m/s with thrust T = 60 kN, drag D = 35 kN, weight W = 120 kN, thrust along the flight path, g = 9.81 m/s².

parts.ask: Find the energy height h_e (m).
Find the specific excess power P_s (m/s, 2 decimals).
Held at constant altitude, find the longitudinal acceleration (m/s², 3 decimals).
sol: P_s = dh/dt + (V/g)dV/dt; with dh/dt = 0, dV/dt = gP_s/V

parts.ask: The minimum time to climb path on an h versus V chart with P_s contours follows:
parts.a: Points where P_s contours touch h_e lines
w: The P_s = 0 contour all the way up
Constant Mach at maximum thrust
Points where h_e lines cross the P_s = 0 contour
sol: Time to change energy is ∫dh_e/P_s, minimized by max P_s at each h_e
Max P_s on each h_e line is where a P_s contour is tangent to that line (Rutowski)

problems.x: Specific excess power is the rate of change of energy height, and it can be spent on climb, acceleration or any mix of the two.

problems.title: Wing and fuselage parasite drag buildup
problems.setup: Estimate C_D0 for a light jet with S_ref = 30 m². Wing: S_wet = 62 m², Re = 10⁷, form factor FF = 1.4. Fuselage: S_wet = 70 m², Re = 10⁸, fineness ratio f = 8 with FF = 1 + 60/f³ + f/400. Use fully turbulent C_f = 0.455/(log₁₀Re)^2.58 (neglect compressibility), interference Q = 1 for both, and add 5% for miscellaneous and leakage drag.

parts.ask: Find the wing skin friction coefficient C_f (5 decimals).
Find the fuselage form factor (4 decimals).
Find total C_D0 (5 decimals).
Why does the fuselage C_f come out lower than the wing C_f?
parts.a: Its greater length raises its Reynolds number
w: Its smaller wetted area lowers C_f
Its form factor directly reduces skin friction
It has more laminar flow than the wing
sol: C_f falls slowly as Re rises; fuselage Re = 10⁸ versus wing 10⁷
Wetted area and FF enter the drag separately as multipliers

problems.x: Component buildup sums C_f·FF·Q·S_wet over components and divides by S_ref, with C_f falling as Reynolds number grows with component length.

problems.title: Fowler flap landing C_Lmax
problems.setup: A transport has clean C_Lmax = 1.4. It adds Fowler flaps with airfoil increment Δc_lmax = 1.3(c'/c), extended chord ratio c'/c = 1.15, over a flapped area ratio S_flapped/S = 0.6, with hinge line sweep Λ_HL = 20°. Use Raymer's ΔC_Lmax = 0.9Δc_lmax(S_flapped/S)cos Λ_HL. Landing W/S = 4500 Pa at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³).

parts.ask: Find the wing ΔC_Lmax from the flaps (3 decimals).
Find the approach speed V_app = 1.3V_stall (m/s).
How do a trailing edge flap and a leading edge slat each change the C_L versus α curve?
parts.a: Flap raises C_L at each α; slat raises stall α
w: Flap raises stall α; slat raises C_L at each α
Both raise the lift slope and lower stall α
Flap lowers the lift slope; slat lowers α_L0
sol: A flap adds effective camber, so α_L0 becomes more negative and C_L rises at every α
A slat delays leading edge separation, so the curve continues to a higher stall angle

problems.x: Trailing edge flaps add camber to raise C_L at a given α, leading edge devices raise the stall angle, and both lower the approach speed.

problems.title: Neutral point, static margin and tail volume
problems.setup: A conventional aircraft has wing S = 20 m², c̄ = 2 m, wing-body lift slope a_wb = 5.0 /rad, wing-body aerodynamic center at h_ac = 0.25c̄. Horizontal tail: S_t = 4.5 m², lift slope a_t = 4.0 /rad, tail arm l_t = 6 m, downwash gradient dε/dα = 0.4, tail efficiency 1. Use h_n = h_ac + V_H(a_t/a_wb)(1 − dε/dα). CG at h = 0.35c̄.

parts.ask: Find the horizontal tail volume coefficient V_H (3 decimals).
Find the stick-fixed neutral point h_n (fraction of c̄, 3 decimals).
Find the static margin (fraction of c̄, 3 decimals).
sol: = 0.574 − 0.35 = 0.224, positive so the aircraft is statically stable

parts.ask: The CG moves to 0.45c̄. Find the V_H needed for SM = 0.10 (3 decimals).

problems.x: Static margin is the distance from the CG aft to the neutral point, and the tail volume coefficient is the main lever for moving the neutral point.

problems.title: Pitch stiffness and elevator trim
problems.setup: An aircraft has total lift slope a = 5.0 /rad (C_L = aα, elevator lift neglected), static margin 0.10, C_m0 = 0.05, and elevator power C_mδe = −1.2 /rad. Convention: α and δe in radians, δe positive trailing edge down, nose-up C_m positive. C_m = C_m0 + C_mα α + C_mδe δe.

parts.ask: Find C_mα (/rad).
With δe = 0, find the trim angle of attack (deg, 2 decimals).
sol: Trim: C_m0 + C_mα α = 0, so α = C_m0/(−C_mα)

parts.ask: Find δe to trim at C_L = 0.8 (deg, 2 decimals; negative is trailing edge up).
Moving the CG forward (larger SM, a and C_m0 held fixed) changes trim at C_L = 0.8 how?
parts.a: More trailing edge up elevator is needed
w: Less trailing edge up elevator is needed
Elevator angle stays the same
Trailing edge down elevator is needed
sol: Larger SM makes C_mα more negative, so nose-down moment at α = 0.16 grows
δe = −(C_m0 + C_mα α)/C_mδe grows more negative: more trailing edge up deflection

problems.x: Pitch stiffness C_mα = −a·SM sets how much elevator each change in trimmed C_L requires, and a forward CG raises that requirement.
